## 1. What you will be able to do

Explain the difference between a provider, product, model family, LLM, and Transformer;
make a first “Hello, world!” model request through OpenRouter, repeat it through
LangChain, and define a model task with DSPy; then run, inspect, and modify a
small deterministic agent in Colab; reproduce it locally; keep secrets out of
artifacts; and distinguish model, runtime, tool, environment, and trace evidence.

**Phase:** Orientation
**Overview:** 20–40 minutes
**Planned unit effort:** 10–16 hours, including typing, experiments,
checks, and a 90–180 minute challenge. Estimates will be recalibrated during authoring.

**Scenario:** help a repair café hand off a dependable launch kit. Make a first
model request, connect it through a framework, check an unsafe suggested fix,
recover a stale notebook, and repair a broken local entry point. Your final
artifact is a launch card another volunteer can reproduce, with inputs and
evidence rather than a screenshot of one successful output.

## 2. Before you begin

Bring project-ready Python: functions, data structures, modules, exceptions, and basic tests. Use the [readiness guide](../../readiness.qmd) to check gaps.

Use the [offline smoke lab](../../../../resources/agent-lab.qmd) to check the
shared package. Work in a clean Colab/Jupyter notebook or a local Conda
environment with Poetry-managed dependencies. Lessons 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 each
make a live OpenRouter request; they need an OpenRouter account, API key, and internet
access. They use the current free-model route; availability and limits can
change. The later offline agent examples still have an offline path.
Keep credentials and personal data out of notebooks, traces, and submitted artifacts.

The first two calls send the same generic, non-sensitive prompt to a remote
model, first directly and then through LangChain. Lesson 0.3 uses a separate
synthetic repair note to demonstrate DSPy. The offline package examples
use synthetic task and tool data; store the API key in Colab Secrets, not in the
notebook.
Local development requires Git and the real project Conda + Poetry environment;
initial installation needs registry access. No GPU is required. Use an explicit
workspace, keep your journal outside temporary runtime storage, and distinguish
notebook success from a verified local installation.

**Working vocabulary:** the task states the requested result; a language model
generates text; an agent system can use model-selected steps and tools; the
harness or runtime authorizes, dispatches, and records those steps. The live
OpenRouter calls reach a real language model. The separate offline loop uses a
deterministic test double, not an LLM. In-process examples are not security
sandboxes. General runtime, tool-boundary, and security engineering arrive in
Units 3, 5, and 15.

## 3. Planned lesson sequence

| Lesson | Evidence you will preserve |
|---|---|
| 1. Introduction to Agentic AI: Models, Agents, and Harnesses | Model-family notes, key vocabulary, returned model ID, and “Hello, world!” response. |
| 2. Connect to Models with LangChain | Returned model ID, response, token usage when available, and provider-route comparison. |
| 3. Program a Model Task with DSPy | Task signature, returned fields, selected model route, and a note on when DSPy is useful. |
| 4. Work Reliably in Colab and Jupyter | Clean restart-and-run transcript. |
| 5. Build a Dependable Local Workspace | Environment report and passing cross-environment smoke test. |

### 1. Introduction to Agentic AI: Models, Agents, and Harnesses

Meet familiar AI products and model families, learn what LLMs and Transformers are, and distinguish an agent from its harness. Then make one “Hello, world!” request through OpenRouter and note which model answered.

### 2. Connect to Models with LangChain

Repeat the first model request through LangChain, inspect its message and metadata, and compare OpenRouter routing with direct OpenAI, Gemini, and Cohere connections.

### 3. Program a Model Task with DSPy

Explain why DSPy was created, define a task with a signature, and make a model call through OpenRouter while identifying direct-provider alternatives.

### 4. Work Reliably in Colab and Jupyter

Inspect notebook state, execution order, package installation, files, runtime resets, and reproducibility. Recover a notebook whose apparent success depends on stale variables and an unrecorded package version.

### 5. Build a Dependable Local Workspace

Create the course environment with Git, Conda, `Poetry`, Python, pytest, Ruff, type checking, and environment-variable configuration on Windows, macOS, or Linux. Run the same smoke test locally and in Colab.

## 4. Challenge preview: Prove the Lab Is Ready

Repair a deliberately stale notebook and broken local project, run the tiny agent from clean state, reject an unsafe AI-generated fix, and submit a launch card containing versions, commands, outputs, and unresolved limitations.

The draft challenge includes a deliberately stale notebook, a CLI that ignores its
input path, independent fresh-process checks, three progressive hints, and a
hidden solution. It is not yet a released assessment. The contract requires
explicit input paths, current operands, denial before tool effects, and an
actionable failure instead of a fabricated missing input. Local setup and
clean-kernel evidence are separate gates. A successful-looking output alone will
not establish reliability: preserve inputs, limits, behavior, and failed cases.

## 5. Suggested stopping points

Plan one session per lesson. Before changing an implementation, write a prediction;
after each session, record what ran, what failed, what changed, and what remains
unverified. Save a clean run and an architecture note before attempting the challenge.
Finish with a retrospective on quality, failures, latency, cost, and safety.

Suggested breaks: after the first model call (Lesson 1); after the LangChain
comparison and DSPy task (Lessons 2–3); after a clean notebook run
(Lesson 4); and after the local environment report (Lesson 5). Save evidence at
each break. Pause setup work on an unavailable registry rather than silently
substituting a different environment. The challenge finishes with a comparison
against direct arithmetic and an explicit list of unverified claims.
